subject: math
cluster: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable
description: Students interpret and compare data distributions by describing their shape (symmetric, skewed left, skewed right, uniform, with peaks or gaps), measuring center (mean $\bar{x}$ and median), and measuring spread (range, interquartile range $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$, and standard deviation). They identify outliers using the $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ rule, explain how an extreme data point shifts the mean far more than the median and inflates the range and standard deviation, and choose which center and spread measures best summarize a given data set in context.
subSkills: Describe the shape of a distribution from a dot plot, histogram, or box plot (symmetric, skewed right, skewed left, uniform, bimodal, gaps and clusters)
Compute the mean $\bar{x}=\frac{\sum x_i}{n}$ and the median of a data set
Identify outliers with the $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ fences: below $Q_1-1.5\cdot\text{IQR}$ or above $Q_3+1.5\cdot\text{IQR}$
Explain and quantify the effect of an outlier on mean vs. median and on range/IQR/standard deviation
Choose the resistant measures (median, IQR) for skewed data and (mean, standard deviation) for roughly symmetric data, with justification
Compare the centers and spreads of two distributions in context

problemArchetypes.name: Describe shape from a display
problemArchetypes.example: A dot plot of quiz scores piles up at the high end with a long tail toward the low scores. Describe the shape of the distribution. (Answer: skewed left.)

problemArchetypes.name: Compute center and spread
problemArchetypes.example: For the data set $\{4, 6, 6, 7, 9, 12\}$, find the mean, the median, the range, and the IQR. (Answers: mean $=\frac{44}{6}=\frac{22}{3}$, median $=6.5$, range $=8$, $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1=9-6=3$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Outlier test with the $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ rule
problemArchetypes.example: A data set has $Q_1=12$, $Q_3=20$, so $\text{IQR}=8$. Is the value $35$ an outlier? (Upper fence $=20+1.5\cdot 8=32$; since $35>32$, yes it is an outlier.)

problemArchetypes.name: Effect of an outlier on center and spread
problemArchetypes.example: The values $\{8, 9, 10, 11, 12\}$ have mean $10$ and median $10$. Replace $12$ with $42$. What happens to the mean and the median? (Mean rises to $\frac{80}{5}=16$; median stays $10$. The mean is pulled toward the outlier; the median resists it.)

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the appropriate measures
problemArchetypes.example: Home prices in a neighborhood are strongly skewed right by a few mansions. Which measure of center and which measure of spread best summarize the data, and why? (Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the skew and extreme values.)

problemArchetypes.name: Compare two distributions in context
problemArchetypes.example: Class A scores have median $78$, $\text{IQR}=6$; Class B has median $78$, $\text{IQR}=20$. Same center, but compare the spread and what it means about consistency. (Class B is far more variable; scores are less consistent.)

Easy.description: Single-concept recall and one-step computation on a small, clean data set (about $5$ to $7$ values, often pre-sorted). Identify shape from a clear display, or compute one statistic (mean, median, or range), or apply a one-line definition. No outlier fences yet.
constraints: Data set has $\le 7$ values, integers, already sorted or trivially sorted
Asks for exactly one statistic or a shape label from an unambiguous display
Median lands on an actual data value (odd $n$); mean is an exact integer or simple fraction
No IQR fence computation and no comparison of two data sets

Medium.description: Multi-step computation: find quartiles and IQR, OR apply the full $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ outlier test, OR compute how the mean and median each change when one value is altered. Connects center/spread to shape (e.g. mean > median implies skewed right).
constraints: Data set has $8$ to $12$ values requiring correct quartile placement
Requires $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$ and may require both upper and lower fences
Quantifies the before/after effect of changing or removing one extreme value
Links the relationship between mean and median to the shape of the distribution

Hard.description: Reasoning and justification in context: compare two distributions on shape, center, and spread together; decide which center/spread measures are appropriate and defend the choice; reason about standard deviation qualitatively; or solve a backward problem (find a missing value given a target mean or determine what value would make a point an outlier).
constraints: Compares two data sets or two displays across shape, center, AND spread
Requires choosing resistant vs. non-resistant measures with a written justification
May reason about standard deviation as relative spread without a heavy formula computation
May be a reverse problem: solve for an unknown data value given a target mean, or find the boundary value at an outlier fence

difficultyRubric._split: This standard is conceptually broad (shape + center + spread + outliers + measure selection), so it is authored as a tier1 + tier2 pair. tier1 covers Easy to Medium: describing shape, computing a single center/spread statistic, finding IQR, and the basic $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ outlier test. tier2 covers Medium to Hard: quantifying outlier effects on mean vs. median, comparing two distributions, justifying the choice of resistant measures, qualitative standard deviation, and reverse problems. No item overlap between tiers.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses the direction of skew, naming it for the side with the bulk of the data instead of the side with the tail
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls a distribution with a long left tail 'skewed right' because most points sit on the right

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Believes the mean is always the best or only measure of center, even for skewed data with outliers
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Recommends the mean and range for strongly skewed home-price data instead of the median and IQR

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Computes IQR as the range or as $Q_3+Q_1$ instead of $Q_3-Q_1$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports $\text{IQR}=Q_3+Q_1$ (e.g. $9+6=15$) or the full range instead of $Q_3-Q_1=3$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Uses a fixed cutoff or the wrong multiplier for outliers instead of the $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ fences
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls any value more than $2\cdot\text{IQR}$ above the mean an outlier, or uses $Q_3+\text{IQR}$ as the fence, giving the wrong verdict

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Thinks an outlier shifts the median as much as the mean, not recognizing the median as resistant
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims that replacing $12$ with $42$ in $\{8,9,10,11,12\}$ raises both the mean and the median

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets to sort the data before finding the median or quartiles
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the middle value of the unsorted list as the median (e.g. takes the $3$rd entry as listed rather than the $3$rd smallest)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses measures of center with measures of spread
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Names the mean or median when asked for a measure of spread, or names the IQR when asked for center

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Assumes equal centers mean equal distributions, ignoring spread
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Concludes two classes with the same median performed identically even though one has $\text{IQR}=6$ and the other $\text{IQR}=20$

_comment_itemCounts: Authored as a tier1 + tier2 pair because the standard spans shape, center, spread, outliers, and measure selection. tier1 = Easy->Medium, tier2 = Medium->Hard, no item overlap. lesson 5+5, quiz 8.
